questions.q: State two key properties of the normal distribution curve.
questions.answer: The normal distribution curve is symmetric (bell-shaped) about its mean $\mu$, and the total area under the curve equals 1. (Other valid properties: mean = median = mode; the curve is asymptotic to the horizontal axis.)

questions.q: Explain what it means for the normal distribution curve to be "asymptotic" to the horizontal axis.
questions.answer: It means the curve approaches the horizontal axis as $x\to\pm\infty$ but never actually touches or crosses it — the probability density gets arbitrarily close to zero but is never exactly zero for any finite $x$.

questions.q: State one similarity and one difference between the normal distribution and the discrete uniform distribution.
questions.answer: Similarity: both are probability distributions in which the total probability sums (or integrates) to 1. Difference: the normal distribution is continuous and bell-shaped, with values clustering near the mean, while the discrete uniform distribution is discrete and every outcome has equal probability.

sections.heading: The normal approximation to the binomial distribution

questions.q: A random variable $X\sim B(200,0.4)$ is to be approximated by a normal distribution. State the mean and variance to use, and check the approximation is valid (both $np$ and $n(1-p)$ should exceed 5).
questions.answer: $np=200(0.4)=80$ and $n(1-p)=200(0.6)=120$, both exceed 5, so the approximation is valid. Use $X\approx N(80,48)$, since $\text{Var}(X)=np(1-p)=200(0.4)(0.6)=48$.

questions.q: A random variable $X\sim B(150,0.5)$ is to be approximated by a normal distribution. State the mean and variance to use, and check the approximation is valid.
questions.answer: $np=150(0.5)=75$ and $n(1-p)=150(0.5)=75$, both exceed 5, so the approximation is valid. Use $X\approx N(75,37.5)$, since $\text{Var}(X)=np(1-p)=150(0.5)(0.5)=37.5$.

sections.heading: Solving for unknown parameters of a normal distribution

questions.q: A random variable $X\sim N(\mu,36)$ satisfies $P(X<50)=0.8413$, given $\Phi(1)\approx0.8413$. Find $\mu$.
questions.answer: $\sigma=6$, and the $z$-value corresponding to probability $0.8413$ is $z=1$. So $\dfrac{50-\mu}{6}=1$, giving $\mu=50-6=44$.

questions.q: A random variable $X\sim N(\mu,49)$ satisfies $P(X<66)=0.9772$, given $\Phi(2)\approx0.9772$. Find $\mu$.
questions.answer: $\sigma=7$, and the $z$-value corresponding to probability $0.9772$ is $z=2$. So $\dfrac{66-\mu}{7}=2$, giving $\mu=66-14=52$.

questions.q: A random variable $X\sim N(\mu,25)$ satisfies $P(X<40)=0.9332$, given $\Phi(1.5)\approx0.9332$. Find $\mu$.
questions.answer: $\sigma=5$, and the $z$-value corresponding to probability $0.9332$ is $z=1.5$. So $\dfrac{40-\mu}{5}=1.5$, giving $\mu=40-7.5=32.5$.

sections.heading: A well-designed word problem: setting a pass mark for an exam

questions.q: This question has two parts. Scores on a standardized exam are normally distributed with mean $\mu=68$ and standard deviation $\sigma=12$. The exam board wants to set a pass mark so that exactly the top $10\%$ of students pass, and is told that the $z$-value corresponding to the top $10\%$ (i.e. $P(Z>z)=0.10$) is $z\approx1.2816$. (a) Find the pass mark, to the nearest whole number. (b) A student scores 90 on the exam. Find their $z$-score, and state whether they are in the top 10%.
questions.answer: (a) $x=\mu+z\sigma=68+1.2816(12)\approx68+15.38\approx83$ (to the nearest whole number). (b) $z=\dfrac{90-68}{12}=\dfrac{22}{12}\approx1.833$. Since a score of 90 exceeds the pass mark of approximately 83 (and $z\approx1.833>1.2816$), this student IS in the top 10%.
